summary:
Lithuania permits a trans visitor to enter and move about without any LGBT-specific entry screening, but the country offers no working route to legal gender recognition. Article 5.1 of the Civil Code grants unmarried adults the right to change gender through medical intervention, and no implementing legislation has ever been adopted. The Lithuanian Gay League counts the resulting gap at 18 years; the public broadcaster counts 17. Both figures describe the same condition: a statutory right with no procedure behind it.

The courts declined to close that gap twice in 2025. In August the Ukmergė Chamber of the Vilnius Regional District Court suspended a civil case concerning the amendment of civil-status gender documents and referred to the Constitutional Court the question of whether the relevant provisions comply with the Constitution. In September the Constitutional Court declined to examine the referral, leaving the absence of legal provisions for changing gender markers and personal identification codes in official documents intact. A trans visitor whose passport carries a mismatched marker has no domestic legal mechanism to correct it before or during travel.

Violence-incitement against LGBT people is expressly prohibited under Section 170(3) of the Criminal Code, and a 2010 preliminary investigation found that 160 of roughly 180 recorded hate-speech incidents, most of them online, targeted the LGBT community; perpetrators were usually fined. Enforcement machinery remains thin. ILGA-Europe's 2025 Annual Review records a systemic lack of targeted support for LGBTI hate-crime victims, and the Seimas Ombudsperson found in April 2024 that police failed to guarantee the LGBT community's right to peaceful assembly after an inadequate response to hostile provocateurs at an LGL gathering, recommending measures to secure effective assembly rights.

Pride events have been obstructed repeatedly. Baltic Pride in 2010 was halted by a court shortly before it began, allowed back one day prior, then held under heavy policing amid violence with 12 protesters arrested; the 2013 march required litigation through every judicial instance to proceed, and drew about 500 participants and 28 arrests. Numbers have since grown to roughly 10,000 at the 2019 Vilnius Pride and 5,000 in 2023, and a visitor joining a Pride event should expect counter-protest and a documented history of police failure to hold that line.

Discrimination in daily life is well evidenced. Reporting by the public broadcaster in May 2025 documented trans people describing open ridicule, isolation and psychological abuse at work, with experts describing systemic labour-market discrimination. The Office of the Equal Opportunities Ombudsperson's 2024 national review, the second after 2019, covers document changes, healthcare barriers, labour-market discrimination, data protection and public attitudes, and records both the absence of a legal framework and the absence of any strategic approach to trans rights.

Marriage is restricted to opposite-sex couples under Article 38 of the 1992 Constitution and Article 3.12 of the Civil Code. On 17 April 2025 the Constitutional Court ruled that the absence of legal regulation of partnership institutions, including for same-sex couples, contradicts the Constitution, and allowed same-sex couples to register partnerships through the courts until the Seimas adopts a comprehensive law. A trans visitor travelling with a partner should not expect the partnership to be recognised on arrival: no visa, entry or residence provisions specific to LGBT visitors are set out, and recognition of a foreign partner depends on Lithuanian civil-status rules rather than on any visitor regime. Foreign same-sex spouses were separately guaranteed residence permits by the Constitutional Court in January 2019, following the European Court of Justice judgment in Coman.
tangentialFactors:
Legislative hostility toward trans people has been a live current rather than a closed chapter. In September 2013 the Seimas considered five bills including an outright ban on gender reassignment, premised on the assertion that gender is determined genetically at conception, alongside a same-sex adoption ban, fines of up to €1,800 for organisers of events said to denigrating constitutional moral values, and legalisation of anti-gay speech. Two separate attempts to criminalise the public propagation of homosexual relations, carrying fines of 2,000 to 10,000 litas, failed in 2011 and 2013. The bills did not pass, but they establish the level of parliamentary argument a trans visitor's status has been subject to.

Expression restrictions targeting minors took effect in 2009 when Parliament overrode President Adamkus's veto on the Law on the Protection of Minors by 87-6, an amendment Amnesty International called a huge step backwards. The anti-LGBT clauses were replaced in December 2009 with a broader ban on information promoting conceptions of marriage or family other than the constitutional one; that provision was used to restrict a 2013 Vilnius Pride advertisement to night-time broadcast with an adult-content logo and to age-label and then ban the children's book Gintarinė širdis in 2014, a ban the ECHR Grand Chamber found contrary to Article 10 in January 2023. On 18 December 2024 the Lithuanian Constitutional Court struck the anti-LGBT provisions down as violating Article 25 freedom of speech.

Public assembly and counter-protest remain the sharpest physical risk. Overturning a 2007 refusal by Vilnius City Council, a 2010 court reversal and heavy policing set the pattern; over 10,000 people also protested against partnership legislation in Vilnius in May 2021. Set against that, participation in Pride has risen rather than fallen.

ILGA-Europe's 2025 review also records the prosecution of former MP Gražulis for anti-LGBTI ridicule being complicated by his immunity as a Member of the European Parliament, and the four-year wait endured by LGBTI asylum seekers from Cameroon before they were granted protection amid dire camp conditions, including the conviction of a psychologist for coercing asylum seekers into sexual acts. Neither case concerns visitors directly, but both indicate where official protection machinery fails.

Lithuania is comparatively permissive on entry itself: same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1993, the age of consent was equalised at 14 in 2003 for EU accession and raised to 16 in 2010 regardless of orientation, and no entry or visa rule turns on gender identity or sexual orientation.
localsOnly:
Residents seeking to amend civil-status gender documents have no statutory route, and personal identification codes remain tied to the unamended marker. The Equal Opportunities Ombudsperson's 2024 national review treats the missing framework and the lack of a strategic approach to trans rights as the governing conditions, with healthcare barriers and data protection listed among the fields it covers.

Workplace treatment is documented in detail. Trans employees describe open ridicule, isolation and psychological abuse, and experts describe labour-market discrimination as systemic rather than incidental.

Adoption remains closed to same-sex couples because marriage is required, and although single applicants are theoretically eligible, adoption by single gay people is not legally possible in practice. President Gitanas Nauseda stated in September 2021 that he would do his best to block adoption demands made by Kaunas Pride organisers. Only 24 same-sex households were declared in the 2011 census.

The Seimas Ombudsperson's April 2024 findings bind police to recommended measures guaranteeing effective assembly rights, and the December 2024 Constitutional Court judgment removed the anti-LGBT clauses of the Law on the Protection of Minors from the statute book. Residents may now register same-sex partnerships through the courts under the 17 April 2025 ruling while the Seimas works on comprehensive legislation.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: whether the Seimas has acted on the 17 April 2025 Constitutional Court partnership ruling, and whether a comprehensive registered-partnership law has been tabled or passed since. The inventory records only that a partnership bill was preliminarily approved 46-17 in May 2017 and still pending in 2019.

Unresolved: whether the suspended Ukmergė Chamber referral was reinstated or otherwise progressed after the Constitutional Court declined to examine it in September 2025, and whether any further civil-status case is before the courts.

Not sourced: bathroom and facilities access, airport or border screening practices that could expose a mismatched passport marker, availability and legality of hormone treatment or other gender-affirming care for short-term visitors, and whether a foreign identity document with a changed marker is accepted by Lithuanian authorities. Nothing in the inventory addresses these directly.

Unresolved: current hate-crime prosecution rates. The only enforcement figures in the inventory are from a 2010 preliminary investigation; no later case-level data is available here.
